utterances.text: Page 45, line 3, you mentioned Edin something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Edin Sulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness who has already testified in the courtroom. Edin Sulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I give the position of the Defence very briefly, please? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could just do it in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Mr. President, I can say that several weeks now that we can call an incident of proceedings, nothing has been done. Nothing has been done to find out what happened with the grattage procedure. I believe that what I understand in any language what you asked was not a confirmation of a doctor on a date or another date, but how this grattage could be explained. Today, we don't know anything because nothing has been done, absolutely nothing. Therefore, the Defence, considering this, the Defence is asking formally a decision from your Chamber so that these exhibits are made inadmissible. We cannot continue in this way. The Defence cannot accept this. And I thank you in advance for this decision that you will take shortly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Stamp, would you -- could the Prosecution call its next Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Could the witness Zdenko Eterovic be brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Eterovic, I assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text will be -- should already by handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Eterovic. Please be seated. Counsel for the Prosecution will be first to examine you. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp. Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Eterovic. Can we begin by stating your name and occupation for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can begin. My name is Zdenko Eterovic. I am currently the judge at the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your employment during the years 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: From 1975, I have been a judge, that is from the very first day of my work until today, except that I have worked on different judge -- different courts of different levels. In 1994, 1995, 1996, I was a judge at the high court of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a judge of the high court of Sarajevo in 1994, in particular, did your role involve participating or directing investigations of certain incidents?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among other tasks at the court, I also did work for an -- as an investigative judge or investigating incidents, as we called it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately how many incidents involving shelling where there were civilian casualties that you investigated in the period September 1992 to August 1994? And I am going to ask you to give us an approximation.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: For me, the word "incident," to say that is too small a term. I would translate it as an unfortunate accident, incident. But I took part in about 300 to 400 of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you recall approximately how many of these incidents - if you pardon my using the expression - you investigated involving civilian deaths of more than two persons within that period, 1992 September to 1994 August?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you, of course, the exact number, but it is certain that it was from 100 to 150 of such investigations that I conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to take you to two investigations in particular. Do you recall participating in an investigation on the 20th of January -- I beg your pardon, the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall where this investigation took place or where you went to?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: It was conducted in the municipality of Novi Grad. The neighbourhood is called Alipasino Polje. At the time these streets were called Cetinska Street and Klara Zetkin Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you write a report in respect of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After each investigation, there would be a report. We would call it a record of an investigation and this report was also compiled after this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you signed the report that you did?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, Your Honours, could the witness be shown Exhibit 2171C?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the Court be shown that Exhibit as well as Exhibit 2171C.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I take it that you are aware that there appears information in this document which relates to protected witnesses, so, therefore, we have to deal with it very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I just wanted to use this occasion in order not to interrupt Mr. Stamp. 49.25: It should be "investigation" instead of "subject."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having perused that document in front of you, do you see your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a copy of your report in respect of your investigation of an incident in Alipasino Polje on the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have in this document referred to casualties. Could you briefly, if you can, tell us what procedures you employed to establish the casualties in respect of this incident.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Like in any other investigation, we used the normal way, which is to ask the witnesses who were at the scene of the incident, then going to the hospital, gathering data at the hospital on who was brought, whoever was dead, whoever was wounded, with all the identification possibilities in order to identify these persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the body of the report, it indicates that you went to -- I beg your pardon -- not that you went to, but that the casualties were taken to the state hospital and the Kosevo hospital. Did you go to those hospitals as part of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After each investigation, these are the only two hospitals --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I apologise. The French interpretation says "State hospital of Kosevo" and we know very well that these are two different things: On one side, state hospital, and on the other side, the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps it is my fault. I'll try to speak a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the list of casualties, do you see the name Goran Todorovic there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see it. It is not on the list. However, of course, I don't know this information. If on the basis of something else it was established that he was also wounded, it is easy to find out. It's easily happened. In Sarajevo, after a shell would land, everybody was trying to find their way out of it. So if there was a shell that landed and if this man, Todorovic, was either injured or perhaps if he was able to do it himself or perhaps assisted by someone, maybe he went to a field surgery or maybe he went by himself to a hospital and did not report his name to the duty doctor, it is possible that he may well have been injured during this incident, this event, and that he is not on the list. What I believe and what I can claim is that these people who are on the list were certainly injured and unfortunately died, and the list could only be longer, not shorter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, in the course of your investigation of that incident, go to a military medical institution at the former Viktor Bubanj barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks is called Viktor Bubanj, but I never went. Not only regarding this investigation, I never went. I don't think there was a surgery there. But I am sorry, I have to add it is not close by. Viktor Bubanj barracks, as the crow flies, is at least 500 metres, if not a full kilometre, further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that it is possible that a witness might not be on the list, if he went to a field hospital. So, may I ask you this: If this -- may I rephrase what I said. You indicated earlier that it was possible that if a victim had been treated at a field hospital and not at any other hospital that you went to, he might not be on the list. So if in fact this person, Goran Todorovic, was treated at that medical facility, you would not have had received that information from that facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to intervene in order to obtain something precise. We never spoke of field hospitals in Sarajevo so far. Could Mr. Stamp be a little more precise as to which hospital he was referring? We never spoke of field hospitals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was the witness who spoke about it and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter may have inadvertently used the word "field hospital" as opposed to a surgery, an improvised surgery. I am sorry, I heard it in another language, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion about words used also by the interpretation. Perhaps if you but the question to the witness again, keeping in mind the observation made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier -- you said earlier that sometimes persons injured in a variety of incidents may be treated at various medical facilities which were outside of your purview of investigation. Could you please clarify what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: In wartime Sarajevo, there were two hospitals. One was Kosevo hospital and the other one was state hospital. It changed the name from "French" to "army" to the state hospital. At this time I believe it was called the state hospital. So there were two hospitals. Apart from these two hospitals, there were no other hospitals. There were no field surgeries. There were just outpatient clinics. There were perhaps 10 or 20 of them. I can't tell you the exact number. But each municipality had their own clinic. Now, where exactly it was in the city, in that part of the city, I don't know because I live in Marin Dvor and I would know exactly where the outpatient clinic in Marin Dvor would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This clarifies the point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it is not necessary when it is clear for everyone that things have been clarified, we should not further interrupt Mr. Stamp in his examination of the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you are saying, can we take it that had this person Goran Todorovic been treated at a medical facility in the vicinity of the Viktor Bubanj barracks, you would not have received information from that barracks since you did not go there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it is the first time I hear from you that there was a clinic at that barracks. I know about the barracks, but the answer -- my answer is certainly that I wouldn't have known. I wouldn't have known that Goran Todorovic was wounded if he had gone to such a clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You wrote in your report that two -- that three shells impacted but two caused casualties, one at Cetinska Street and the other at Klara Zetkin Street. And you indicated in your report where persons were injured. At the time you wrote your report, had you had an opportunity to interview any of the children who were injured in this incident, to find out exactly where they were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but reading of this question during the -- in the transcript seems not very clear to me and I believe that there is confusion between one, two and three shells. Could we please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if it is not clear, the witness will tell us. If it would be confusing, the Chamber will interfere, but would you please let Mr. Stamp -- make it possible for Mr. Stamp to examine the witness with as little interruptions as possible. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want you to clarify, Mr. Eterovic, is whether or not you were able to confirm from the children themselves where exactly they were playing in front of which building they were playing at the time when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I was able to establish this, unfortunately, based on the parts of the bodies of the children on the spot, including some -- what they were wearing and shoes, where they were on the snow, but unfortunately, I did not speak to the children. They were taken to the hospital. There were not very many witnesses. There was a lot of fear at the time in that location. So I remember that -- when I remember that incident, what I remember is a great deal of silence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate - and we are moving on now very quickly - in an investigation of an incident of the 4th of February, 1994, in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was in Dobrinja I. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you write a report in respect to your investigation of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, Mr. President, Your Honours, with your leave tender to the witness Exhibit P2247B.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted. Could you please assist, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your report in respect to the incident of the 4th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is my report. It is a report on investigation. Report on on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in respect to the casualties, which hospitals or medical facilities did you visit as part of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja is a very specific locality in Sarajevo, which is in itself in a blockade, like the whole of Sarajevo, so you can imagine there was a mini blockade of Dobrinja only linked by one street to Sarajevo. So what they had was a kind of clinic. They called it a hospital. So, in the first instance, after we conducted our usual on-site investigations, we went to their so-called hospital. I call it a clinic. After that, we went to the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to a doctor or the doctors at the Dobrinja medical facility?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I remember in that medical facility in Dobrinja that doctor, he founded it. I don't know his name but he is an Arab. There were two nurses and himself. He was the one who gave me most of the information, along with the nurses, and of course everything we were able to see for ourselves. It is a very small clinic, a very small facility, which only has two rooms, very small, and one small office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you comment, if you can, about what you observed when you went there in respect of your observations of this incident. What was the scene like at the Dobrinja hospital or, if you will, clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this investigation, this on-site investigation was chaotic. It was probably one of the most difficult ones, professionally speaking, because Dobrinja anyway was a kind of locality which suffered a great deal in the war. There were many dead, many wounded, and in this hospital, I can only remember one, for instance, situation when we are looking over the dead and we are looking at some kind of wood store, they were just putting the dead there. And the wounded were everywhere: on the tables, on the floors. In this office, there were wounded people lying there. People were going in, asking for their nearest and dearest. It was a very chaotic situation in that clinic which, of course, wasn't surprising considering its size and considering the number of the wounded and the dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the doctor indicate to you whether they were able to treat everyone who had been injured?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: No. He immediately said that he had sent to Kosevo hospital some six or some three -- I am sorry. I would have to check that in the documents, these patients to the Kosevo hospital, because he thought he was not able to provide treatment. But the others were there. Of course, the wounded -- it was very hard to get from Dobrinja to Sarajevo and it was very risky to even come to an on-site investigation, let alone transfer the wounded over there. So the very first aid hospitalization was done by this doctor with his medical personnel. And then what he would do is he would sent people perhaps later to the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate what he could do in those circumstances with persons who were only slightly injured from the incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Those who were only slightly wounded, and I saw this personally, he would clean their wounds, dress them, and release them immediately. A while ago you mentioned Mr. Todorovic. There were, of course, more people who were wounded, but they would be only slightly wounded and they would have been released by the time I arrived or even during my investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any record being kept in respect to those people who could be dressed and released immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Probably those who were only cut or slightly wounded were not recorded. This clinic had its log book, its register, and the data would be entered, their details. But those who are only slightly wounded would not undergo this procedure because of the enormous number of people there. They were lying on the floor. It was a difficult to walk. So only those who were more seriously wounded were recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at your report, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, Judge, if I referred to you as Doctor, but could you please --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- look at page -- where is it? Page 2 of your report. In the middle of that page, do you see the name "Sabahudin Ljusa"?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is on the statement that the following individuals received first aid but died on admission to Kosevo hospital. And if you look on the same page below, in the long list, at number five, do you see the name --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the question please be repeated, Mr. President? We didn't get it in the French booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, please look at the name Sabahudin Ljusa at number 3, in the middle of the page, and the name Ljusa Sabahudin at number five just below. Do you see them? I beg your pardon, Judge.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, it is a compliment if someone calls you a doctor, so thank you very much. Yes, I have seen it. It is obviously a mistake made by me, but the error would be due to the chaos prevailing at the time both in the hospital and in my head. I assert that ultimately - although I never saw - but we did take photographs so we are certain that nine people were killed. Thank God Sabahudin Ljusa is alive, and I learned that later. But when I was drawing up this report, obviously, I didn't notice because of the data I received from the hospital that I listed the same person as both killed and wounded. However, because of the number of casualties and the chaos that was prevailing there at the time, it is quite possible to make an error of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look at that part of your report under the heading "description of the scene"? And could you read the first paragraph. You need not read it out loud. Read it and I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try. "The shelling occurred at around 11.30. A total of three shells fell. The first three landed almost simultaneously. One hit the window frame in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, it has to be translated by the interpreters. So if you read, if you would do it is bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think that Mr. Stamp indicated to you that if you would just read it in silence, that would be good enough. We all have the text in front of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the first paragraph of that section, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: "In the two rooms of that ground floor flat in which a mosque had been situated and the mejtef during the wartime, a shell stabiliser was not found, neither was any shrapnel found. And the place -- from the place where the landed, the direction was established to be south or south-east from the trajectory of the shell."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You say it was established to be a particular direction. Who established that, Judge, can you say?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: In this case, I reinforced my team because we were told that there were over 100 people killed. So we doubled the usual team. Usually, there were three or four team members, along with me, but in this case, there were at least eight of us because I demanded that we take two ballistic experts with us, unlike the previous on-site investigation where there was only one ballistics expert. Here there were two. One of them was Zlatan Medjedovic, who died a year or two ago, and Mirza Sabljica. They were the ones that told me that the direction -- that that was the direction that had been established. If I may only add something. Establishing the direction is not difficult in itself. We had 300.000 ballistic experts in Sarajevo. We all knew, judging by the remains and the concentration of shrapnel, where the shell had come from. But, of course, I, even though I did have some knowledge of this, I did not establish the direction myself. I actually relied on ballistics experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One thing, if I may try to clarify it for the record, and perhaps you could look at your report, who were the two ballistic experts that accompanied you on this investigation? I think there is an error, Mr. President, Your Honours, in the record, so the question will just clarify it, in the names.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: The chief ballistic expert was Zlatan Medjedovic. He is a person that died about two years ago but he was the most experienced expert at the time. He assistant was Mirza Sabljica. If you compare this to the previous investigation, he was a forensic technician, and he underwent training in this period of time. Zlatan Medjedovic and Mirza Sabljica were the ballistics experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall exactly -- well, you said you were able to establish the direction from which it came, but can you recall exactly who told you the direction that that particular shell which hit the mejtef came from?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: This building, all right. Let me tell you, Zlatko Medjedovic said this. The stabiliser of the third shell was even found stuck there. So it was easy to establish the direction, and they all came from the same direction. All this was established by Zlatko Medjedovic, with the aid of Mirza Sabljica. They used a compass and a pencil or a rod. They had a rod about a metre long which they would put into that small hole, the crater, made by this type of shell when it landed on impact. The impact was in the right wall next to the window frame, so it is much easier to do when dealing with a flat surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the direction that the shell that hit the Muslim primary school? May I rephrase? What was the direction of origin of the shell that hit the Muslim school? Perhaps you may consult your record.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I should look at the report. But it is not a school. A mejtef is a room used by Muslims to perform their religious customs. They had no mosque so they improvised a mosque in this flat. It is possible that children did have some religious education there, but it is not a Muslim school, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This place where there was this improvised mosque, can you just have a look at your record and tell us what was the direction from which that shell had been fired from?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I remember precisely that the shell hit the right-hand side of the window frame of that flat. The direction was established by the ballistics experts because a hole was found there, and they put a rod or a pencil inside and were able to establish precisely from which direction the shell had arrived. They could not tell the distance at that point. They would have to calculate it and then put it in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at your report, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: East, south-east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the examination-in-chief, if it pleases you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be examined, Mr. Eterovic, by counsel for the Defence. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr Eterovic, good day.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, today during your examination-in-chief, you told us that between 1992 and 1995, you carried out 300 to 400 on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of various kinds to be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you clarify when you say "of various kinds"?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, to the second question, I responded that the investigation I carried out, there were two or three dead. Sometimes there were 100, 150. Unfortunately, there were also a lot of suicides, robberies, even traffic accidents, which sounds absurd. So all those investigations were carried out by me, among others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem. I see that one of the court reporters is not hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the French booth asks the witness to slow down and to restart his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just didn't hear you, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To restart his answer and to repeat his answer because we didn't get it, and he is also speaking a bit too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, may I ask you again first to slow down a bit. And apart from that, restart the answer that you gave to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the period from December or November 1992, when I started doing this job, until just before the war and even after the war, that is 1996, I cannot be very precise, of course - the information is somewhere in the court archives - I carried out between 300 and 400 on-site investigations during the war. Of that number, about 100 to 150 related to shelling or sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, when you said "100 to 150 shelling and sniping incidents," are you saying that you drew up a report for each of these on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I personally have all these documents, and had someone asked me to, I would have brought them with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you have this documentation, that is, you say you have -- are you saying you have only records or do you also have accompanying documents?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: No, I am referring only to the records I drew up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were carrying out these on-site investigations, and I am referring to the 100 to 150 you mentioned, were you always accompanied by a team of experts who were competent to give their opinion and their findings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of experts you are referring to. If you mean ballistics experts, in case of shelling incidents, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "ballistics experts if there was a shelling, yes," can you tell us about sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: It varied. With snipers in the beginning, up until mid 1994, we did not carry out on-site investigations

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again interrupt you. When I hear the speed the French booth has to develop, it is really too much. Could you, Mr. Eterovic, look at your screen and not start to answer the question until the text stops moving. Well, I don't have to explain to you, Ms. Pilipovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, you started answering my question with respect to investigations of sniping incidents. You told us that until mid-1994, you did not carry out on-site investigations. Can you tell us more precisely when in 1994 you started carrying out such investigations for sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, I think witness is not getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, but I have to wait. Let me tell you what I was talking about. In the beginning, there were only two investigating judges, myself and another one. Later on, there were three and then four. And we simply did not manage to find the time to look into everything that was going on in Sarajevo. And for this reason, the president of the court had a sort of in-house agreement with us investigating judges and this was that we should carry out on-site investigations when it was safe to do so, although this sounds very cruel, but only when more than two or three people were killed. It was only in mid-1994, as far as I can recall, that UNPROFO initiated the carrying out of on-site investigations in sniping incidents. Let me add something: This does not mean we were not allowed to go out and carry out an on-site investigation if there was a sniping incident. So sometimes this did happen, but I don't remember myself having done that before mid 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you told us that you carried out on-site investigations in cases of shelling incidents and that there were 100 or 150 of those, could you tell us the time? Was this in 1992 to 1994, or do you allow that this might have been between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't feel that this is important, but, yes, it is possible that 1995 entered into this period. In 1995, there was less shelling, so it is possible that this number would include 1995 as well. But the number of incidents in 1995 would have been very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could you find a suitable moment in one of the next minutes to conclude just for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To my learned friend's question, you responded that you did not know that there was a clinic in the Viktor Bubanj barracks as far as you know. Can you tell us, do you know what there was there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a military prison and a military court which I never entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, you told us that in the barracks Viktor Bubanj there was a military prison and a military court. Could you tell us as a judge with many years of experience and at that time an investigating judge, what was your cooperation with military authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Cooperation of the military court with the civilian courts, if we call them that way, was non-existent. There was no joint cooperation or there was no need for one. They were competent, according to law, for everything that was going on on the front line and in the army. While the civilian courts, where I worked, and of course municipal courts, within their area of competence, worked for the civilian population, that is, for civilian offences, if we can call them that, offences against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, would you agree with me if I say in the period from 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, but we will concentrate on the period between 1992 and 1994, that in the area of Sarajevo, there was a war?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we won't agree on that. Because "war," it would mean that I had participated in the war. War is a war between two armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, would you agree with me that in the period from 1992 on to 1993, 1994, in the area of the city of Sarajevo, and I mean its centre and its -- and greater Sarajevo, specifically in 1992, 1993, 1994, there were three armies: There was BH army, there was the VRS and there was also the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: If you are saying there were three armies, that is correct. And it is also true that these three armies were in Sarajevo or around it, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information or knowledge that these three armies were at war with each other in that area and the territory of the city of Sarajevo and that there was combat activity between these three armies?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: There were no combats between these three armies. There were -- on one side, there was one army, and then two on the other side. In Sarajevo itself, there was no combat. In the Sarajevo itself, there was never combat. There was combat outside Sarajevo. The difference is considerable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, when you say that in Sarajevo there was no combat, would you agree with me if I say that in the city of Sarajevo, the BH army, its personnel, and I mean the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the BH army, that the army, the 1st Corps of BH army, had 11 brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I haven't got a clue. I really truly say I don't have a clue about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that this army was located in that part of Sarajevo, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't. Again, I won't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I won't agree with you because in Sarajevo there were a few barracks that we knew, of course, but the soldiers, apart from the duty services, were not at all in the barracks unless, of course, they were on the front lines, but they were going home. So to your question, if I answered "yes," that would mean that all of the armies were located in that barracks, which isn't true.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: When you say that if you answered yes to my question that that would mean that all the army was in the barracks and that was not true, could you perhaps tell me where were these soldiers? Where were the troops.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely because I do not know. But I can tell you approximately that the area where I live, which is the centre part of Marin Dvor, I know that in Marsal Tito barracks, there were some troops, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that in the former Radio Danijel Osman was a HQ, I think, of the 1st Corps, but I can't possibly be certain of that. And -- oh, yes, I am sorry, and, of course, Hotel Zagreb, that is where troops were. It wasn't barracks, there was just a unit that was there. Their accommodation was there. That was near my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to conduct on-site investigations, when you tell us about the investigations that we have reports of, could you tell us who would you inform about this incident, for instance, about this incident that you would conduct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I would not inform anyone. I would not inform anyone. Simply, I was doing my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, not only for these two investigations, but for the other investigations that you conducted between 1992 and 1994, was there UNPROFOR present at these investigations on-site investigations, or any UNPROFOR representatives?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: To start with, UNPROFOR came very rarely to on-site investigations. It was only later, after General Rose came and this incident, that is, Markale, it was mandatory that we would have to inform UNPROFOR unless they already knew about it. So later on, what happened, we would wait for the start of the -- we would wait for the start of the on-site investigation with the UNPROFOR officers. Now, I will tell you another thing. Earlier, we mentioned ballistics expert, and when our ballistics experts went, for instance Zlatko Medjedovic, Borislav Stanko, and others, it never happened that our analysis, our examination of the trajectory of the shell or the calibre of the shell or the position of where it was fired from, it never differed from the UNPROFOR findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about these investigations that you know of where UNPROFOR conducted any investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I can list a number of them. I was -- I can only tell you my own, not these two, not these two investigations that we spoke about. UNPROFOR did not attend these investigations. But UNPROFOR came twice for on-site investigations at Holiday Inn, once in Bistrik, when over 10 people were killed for queueing for water, and UNPROFOR came at least 20 times for incidents relating to sniping of a tram. At times when tram would start working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, if I put it to you that during the proceedings we have heard witnesses who told us that during their mandate in the city of Sarajevo as UN personnel, they had information that members of BH army were shelling parts of Sarajevo, including civilians, water queues and markets. During the investigations, on-site investigations with UNPROFOR, did you have any information from which positions a specific incident happened or shells were fired from or fire came from?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I could give you this answer: Naturally that these UNPROFOR teams changed, of course, through their national membership and also they varied in quality. What happened in other on-site investigations, I cannot tell you, I won't tell you and I wouldn't know. But I know that on my on-site investigation, there was never a difference between the ballistics analysis report of my experts and their experts. And let me just finish. There was no on-site investigation where I attended or my team attended, we never found that that there was shelling that came from the positions of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, when we are talking about the incidents of shellings, specifically speaking, I will ask you about these two incidents. You said that you personally never informed anyone about this, what was the determined -- what was the outcome of the investigation, but do you have any information or knowledge as to whether on the level of the city of Sarajevo, and I mean the part which was under the control of the Muslim army, the part that was under the control of the Serb army, of the army of Republika Srpska, was there a mixed committee that would take procedure following incidents that happened?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think the answer reflects what my objection would be. Perhaps the expression "mixed" community or committee is a little bit vague and the question should be a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as I -- well, the question has been answered already. So it is not relevant any more, to pay any more attention to it. So Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed. But I would like to remind also, Mr. Stamp, that this morning when there was an interruption from the Defence side, that I felt that the witness was quite able to tell us if the question was not clear enough to him. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Eterovic, you confirm that you do not know that there were mixed military committees that had their teams which checked incidents and events that you conducted on-site investigations of?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Not only that I don't know, but if there was such a committee or a commission, it is certain that it didn't function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they didn't function, could you tell us why not? Why you said that? Why, if it even existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, unless there is a problem in the translation, the witness first testified that he would have no knowledge about it. Then he said, "If there was such a committee," which confirms again that he doesn't know that it was not functioning. And now you are asking him why it didn't function, which of course asks specific knowledge about both the existence of the committee and reasons why it was not functioning. So, let me just ask you, Mr. Eterovic, would you have any knowledge on the existence or the functioning, apart from perhaps that you didn't see any committee functioning? Apart from that, would you have any knowledge about the existence or the functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Not that it existed or that it functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, you compiled on the 22nd of January a report on the on-site investigation. Could you tell us whether, together with this team which is listed in the report, did you come with them or somebody came before you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: The entire team always arrives together. The entire police, as we called them, the CSB, Security Services Centre, had only one car so nobody could arrive earlier. This on-site investigation, there was a policeman who was a security officer from one of the Public Security stations who was close by. He was only one. He was not a team member. He was a security -- he was providing security for the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, as a judge who is conducting an investigation, you are the person who is giving tasks to the members of your team who is going to do what; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And that is why the on-site investigation report ends with the directives, so to speak, of who is supposed to do what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you compile an on-site investigation and you conclude what is to be found on the site, is it possible for any of the team members to compile a report and draw different conclusions from the ones that you drew? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Literally speaking, no. The answer is, it would not be possible. But apart from my report or my record from the on-site investigation, there is an official report, an official note - an official report - which is compiled by the crime inspector who is also attending the site. So what would be valid would be what is written by the judge. And if there is a considerable difference between the judge's document and the document drew up by the inspector, by the criminal inspector, then my paper would be the one that would be competent. It would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, apart -- in your report on the 29th of January, 1994, what was listed is that persons who were present were also the CSB personnel of the gathering of data of war crimes. Could you tell us when was this department for gathering data and information on war crimes established?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. It was established -- I am not quite sure, but some time during this period of time. It could be a month before or so. It functioned independently. It had nothing to do with the court. We were just asked -- considering that they had technical equipment and it was good for us, we were asked to call them during the on-site investigation. They were not allowed to do anything without me and, in fact, they didn't do anything else apart from filming the site with a video camera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, considering that they were filming with a video camera, what were they -- their qualifications? What was their educational background, these people that you were supposed to inform or that you had to inform in the department for detection and gathering information on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that I informed them. That is what you said. What I said is that we were asked to allow them to attend the site, the on-site investigation. Therefore, an investigative judge never called that department to attend, nor did we need to do that. They were probably informed by the CSB personnel, CSB staff, and they were probably working together with them, possibly being informed what is going on and where in Sarajevo. But I don't know what their qualifications were, their educational background. I wasn't interested in that. I was interested in my investigation team. And they were persons who attended the on-site investigation with the authorisation of the president of my court. And in fact, they didn't assist me in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, on the 28th of November, 2001, you gave a statement to the Prosecutor's office. In your statement, on page 1, you said that it was from witness statements that you received information, specifically speaking, about the incident of the 22nd of January. My question is: In this situation, did you speak to witnesses, that is, eyewitnesses of the events?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I already answered that -- the Prosecutor's question. We tried to gather evidence to find out what happened. And it was two-fold: First of all, through witnesses, in which case they would be listed in the report. And, of course, on the basis of the traces on the site of the incident. So I remember -- I don't have the report before me but I do remember that certainly there was one or more witnesses, but I remember one witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, as a judge, did you, and specifically we are talking about the incident of the 22nd of January, did you have any information that in the area of Alipasino Polje there was a factory which was manufacturing ammunition, which was making ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I would like to take you to Sarajevo so that you can see this part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked you if you knew.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know and I doubt that there was a factory there because, objectively speaking, it is impossible to have that in that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information or knowledge that in the area where you said three shells landed - and we are talking about Klara Zetkin and Cetinska Street - there was a military facility where a military unit called Kulin Ban was located?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Kulin Ban is a Croatian unit where my brother was. He died last year. And I claim that he -- they were never there, but they were in Marvin Dvor near the railway station, but in this location, there was not a single military unit. I claim this responsibly. The closest one to this location would have been military unit Viktor Bubanj. But as the crow flies, it would be 500 to a full kilometre from there. And three huge skyscrapers are in between this location and Viktor Bubanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, you said that the unit where your brother was, that is the Croatian Defence Council, that that was located in Marin Dvor. Now, if I put it to you that before this Tribunal there was a witness who testified that he was seriously wounded in the incident, he said that at the entrance to the building where he lived, that there was also a detachment called Kulin Ban and that, every morning, they used their APCs to go to the front lines, would you agree with me that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am very hesitant because I want to assist with the expedition, but that is not a correct quote before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am certain, Ms. Pilipovic, that you have the source nearby so that we can -- if you refer to this testimony, who testified. Because it is not in my recollection, but if you would give me perhaps the name of the witness, we could certainly look at it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said Muhamed Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a literal text of the testimony in this respect, but let me just see to find the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague will find it in the transcript while I continue, part of the quote so that we don't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. And I would like to be informed about the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, in relation to the area of the square where the incident took place, how far is the hill of Mojmilo from that spot?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Which square are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The square where the incident took place. I am referring to Klara Zetkin Street.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but there is no square there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that those streets surround a square, but I am asking you in relation to Klara Zetkin Street, could the hill of Mojmilo be seen from there and how far was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be seen from that spot for the simple reason that it is surrounded by skyscrapers. In my opinion, Mojmilo is quite close, perhaps some 500 metres, because that is the last phase of Alipasino Polje. The next phase in the direction of Dobrinja is Mojmilo. So it is approximately 500 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Cetinska Street and the incident that took place in front of number 3, can you tell us, from that position, is the hill of Mojmilo visible and how far is it from there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I have just answered this question. It cannot be seen, and I think it is 500 metres away but not towards the west. Mojmilo is more to the left so that would be south-west, not west.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence wishes to have the witness shown document P2172, which is a Prosecution Exhibit, and would like to ask the witness to identify on this photograph the hill of Mojmilo. The photograph can be placed on the ELMO and the Defence -- the Defence will hand it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, at the same time, I would like to remind you that you spent already a bit more time than the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only few more questions and I will try to finish as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the meantime, I believe that one of the references that you are looking for is page 7067, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only photograph number 2. There is no name on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, if you can, would you please put the photograph on the ELMO. It says photo 2. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that at the bottom of this photograph, in the direction of the lamp posts, the hill of Mojmilo is visible?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, partly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in the -- in 1994, this hill was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: This part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Eterovic, bearing in mind your profession, were you informed that on the territory of the city of Sarajevo and especially in the area of Bogusevac, it was established that there was a pit called Kazani? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: The answer is, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about this, you personally?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge. I have only second-hand knowledge, what I heard from my colleagues who spoke to me of crimes which "we," in quotation marks, had committed in Kazani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we" in quotation marks --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't commit any crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you say "we," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I was a regular judge of the high court in Sarajevo of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that this answer should be sufficient for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you as a judge try any perpetrators of crimes committed in the Bogusevac area?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where Bogusevac is. If you are referring to Kazani, no, this was done by the military court, not our court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that they were tried by a military court, so the military court tried members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. First, I get some diverting information as far as the source is concerned and since it does not appear in the transcript, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please repeat the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, apologise, Mr. President. There are two pages. There is 7961, line 1, where the answer given by the witness, and I can quote it in English: [In English] "Kulin Ban staff was there." Full stop. And there is also page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the counsel. Could he repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English booth couldn't hear you. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is also the page 7957, line 7, when we are talking more specifically of the vehicles, of transport vehicles, Mr. President. And I will find this line since I -- I can quote: [In English] "There was an APC in front of their staff." APC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The whole -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wondering if I could perhaps assist the Court quickly, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The references that the witness made to Kulin Ban, are on the record and they are at a variety of places in the examination-in-chief and in cross-examination. It will probably not be very convenient to identify all of them now, because I have identified some. But I believe if it is an issue that the tenor of his evidence was that it was in Rade Koncara Square which, from his evidence, would have been about 250 metres from his building, there was a unit called Kulin Ban or an office of a unit called Kulin Ban and he saw an APC there. So if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's be -- let's be brief. The way Ms. Pilipovic presented evidence was not properly done. The word she used was, well, let's say a free interpretation of what she thought the evidence -- the testimony had been. So if you think the question is of any importance, we have now located the sources and now by quoting parts of the testimony of earlier witnesses, you, of course, may put the question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not quote the witness's words. I simply interpreted the essence of what Mr. Kapetanovic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we -- you would have been better quoting him because there seems to be some dispute about what the essence was and the objection is, to that extent, sustained. So you may ask questions but then you perhaps would have to quote or to come up with another essence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, do you have any knowledge that in the place where you conducted the on-site investigation, in the vicinity was the headquarters of the military unit called Kulin Ban? Would you simply answer with yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Eterovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just one question, perhaps two. Re-examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said something which you perhaps could clarify. You said you did not inform anyone of the results of your investigation. Perhaps as a translation, could you explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere at this moment. Mr. Stamp, I did write down that on page 71, lines 4 to 7, that the English text says: "I did not inform anyone" and that the French said "rendre compte" which is -- perhaps the interpreters should assist me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not informing and reporting seems at least in the two, in the English and the French, a bit different. So I was wondering there as well what the original language would have been. So it might be a translation issue. I'm sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can explain what was the purpose of his report and what was done with it.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: I did not inform anyone of any on-site investigation, including this one, nor was I supposed to do so. As in every event, the court had to compile a report of the investigation, collect facts, and compile this report and put it in the archives until something is established, and now something is being established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the reports would be compiled and deposited in the archives until a -- until proceedings - I can call it that - can take place? Is that what is done with your report?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: In view of the shelling and sniping incidents, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just quickly for clarification, you referred to UNPROFOR personnel and their reports or their examinations. I take it you are speaking from your personal experience in respect to investigations you conducted where UNPROFOR personnel may have been there or may not have been there at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you it is quite possible they were everywhere. It is possible that they went there before or after and that I had no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Judge El Mahdi has one question for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you, please, if you can tell me in relation to something you said, an incident that you spoke of during your testimony today, and that was the incident of Markale. Were you the investigative judge of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Markale happened on the following day. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. In your reports, you say that mortar shell fragments were sent for ballistic analysis. Do you know where these fragments are kept, what happens to these fragments and where would it be possible to find these fragments?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: After shelling, only fresh shrapnel was collected, unfortunately, and the fresh -- shell stabilisers. All of Sarajevo was covered with shrapnel. We tried, with the help of ballistics experts, to find the fresh remains of the shells we were investigating. They would then take these remains to the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, where an analysis would be carried out. The calibre, the origin, the trajectory, the true direction would be established. And then in the archives of the MUP, they would be put in a plastic bag with a code number so they could be linked to a particular incident. So the answer would be that this shrapnel and the remains of these shells should be in the MUP, in the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So as far as you know, this is also valid for all incidents? Are these fragments still there as far as you know or is it probable to find some of them? Do they still exist? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ETEROVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, they should all still be there, but I myself have not seen this. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Eterovic, this concludes your examination before this Chamber, since I have no further questions for you. May I thank you for having come the long way from Sarajevo knowing that your profession, it might be quite busy, and that you could come to The Hague. And I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Eterovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, let's deal with the documents. May I just try again to do it once myself. We have document 2171C, on-site investigation report; and 2171.1, translation into English. We have P2247B and P2247B.1, also on-site investigation report, and the dot one version translation into English. The first two documents, 2171C and 2171C.1, under seal, admitted into evidence. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is very important that the Defence informs you of something, and this is to do with proceedings and this is to do with the Prosecution piece, 2146. And I would like to just -- 2247. But what I want to say is that the translations are incomplete. I don't know whether this is deliberate or not. But I can just give you an example. This is page 2247B: The original is in Serbian and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...raise the issue with the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just seen it now. I cannot possibly read everything at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you raise the issue with the Prosecution until tomorrow morning and if the Prosecution agrees that parts of the text are not properly translated, I think both parties will inform the Chamber that a new translation is needed in order to have access to the real text of this document. So the Chamber is -- will highly appreciate to hear the outcome of your discussions with the Prosecution. Is there any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. And this is urgent. Thank you very much. Mr. President, the reason why I wanted to inform you of something, and this is -- this is to do with the Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler testimony. I don't know whether we are able to sit until 2.00 or quarter to 2.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am talking about now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have still three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, I am going to speed up. We just received, Mr. President, we just now, this minute, received a document which is called supplemental information sheet which we received from the Prosecution and which is to do with a Lieutenant-Colonel James Cutler. I didn't have time to make copies to hand one to you. But this is a document of two pages of -- containing new pieces of information. None of this has been translated into Serbian. Obviously, we are not able to discuss this with General Galic. And as it happens, as it happens, it is today, the 23rd of May, this is Colonel Cutler arriving in extremis, where he is suddenly remembering that he's had discussions with Henneberry as to what Major Indjic allegedly said. Now, Mr. President, if we had had these pieces of information in our hands as the Rule 75 ter and 67, Rules of Procedure and Evidence -- but I can see that people are leaving and I can understand why. Now, if we had these elements, Mr. President, we would have done our job, we would have been able to examine Major Henneberry. Today we are given these documents at the very moment when we were not able to ask the questions of Major Henneberry and this happens without General Galic being able to be informed in any language possible, this happens a few minutes before the witness comes, and I won't be able to come tomorrow. I think this is inadmissible and I am being very soft with my words, Mr. President. I will not be here tomorrow, I am sorry, But next week. I can see more people arriving. Now I want to have for next week because the least of things is that we can be prepared properly, particularly if we have additional information, which this is -- this happens at the end of the day and it is not very good, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps the Prosecution respond to the observations and objections made by Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that I would like to, Mr. President, I believe that my friend Mr. Mundis will be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the final proofing of the next witness, Lieutenant-Colonel Cutler, there was some information that he provided to us which we have reduced in writing in a supplemental information sheet. Part of the information contained in that sheet was the direct result of myself asking the witness to think overnight about some issues that we wanted to further clarify based on a previous statement he had given to the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a precise moment when he gave this information to you which you have summarised in writing, when exactly? What day, what time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, the information contained in the report partially came as a result of discussions with Colonel Cutler yesterday. Part of the information contained in this report was being literally typed up. I met with him immediately when I departed from the courtroom following the testimony of Mr. Husovic. So in the intervening 90-minute period, I met once again with Mr. Cutler to see if he had been able to recollect some specific information based on questions that were put to him yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well - that's my first question - that the information was not available during or before the testimony given by Mr. Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct. The information was not in our possession prior to the testimony of Mr. Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Also not in -- apart from the written form, but the information as such was not -- had not come to you, not to your ears, not to your eyes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just confer. Is there any other observation you would like to make, because I interrupted you, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would also be fair to point out that in light of the testimony of Mr. Henneberry, we specifically put questions to Mr. Cutler yesterday afternoon. As a result of that, we asked him to spend the evening thinking about these matters and that we would meet with him this morning, which in fact is what we did. At the same time, I will clearly indicate that we specifically directed Mr. Cutler not to discuss this matter with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Cutler about the content of the testimony of the witness Henneberry in more detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We put to him a series of questions not identifying Mr. Henneberry by name, nor did we provide him with even a remote summary of what Mr. Henneberry testified to. We simply put to him a series of questions based on the information that Mr. Henneberry testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may make one additional comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The supplemental information sheet procedure or process is one which the Prosecution has used on numerous occasions throughout the course of this trial. Obviously they have not been provided to the Chamber, just as we don't provide the Chamber with witness statements. The information that is provided in these documents, on several occasions, has also been exculpatory with respect to the accused, General Galic.
